title: Reading Medication Labels and Orders

sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify the key parts of a medication label, including drug name, strength, dosage form, route, and expiration date.
- Interpret common medication orders accurately, including drug, dose, route, and frequency elements and standard abbreviations.
- Recognize incomplete or unclear medication orders that require clarification before use.
- Apply safe practices for verifying patient identity, medication details, and escalating concerns to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a cereal box: the strength is like the serving size printed on the nutrition label — it tells you how much "active stuff" is in one serving, in this case one tablet.

### Question 2

A generic name is like a person's legal name, while the brand name is like a nickname only one company can use. Both mean the same medicine underneath.

### Question 3

A brand name is like the name of a specific company's soda, while the generic name is the flavor that every company's version shares.

### Question 4

The dosage form is the "shape" the medicine comes in — a solid pill (tablet), a powder-filled shell (capsule), or a liquid. The label always says which one it is.

### Question 5

An expiration date is like the "best by" date on milk — after that date, the medicine may not work as well or could be unsafe, so it should not be used.

### Question 6

The NDC is like a product's barcode serial number — it tells you exactly which company made it, which medicine it is, and what size package.

### Question 7

A lot number is like a batch stamp on a loaf of bread — if one batch is bad, the factory can find every loaf made in that same batch and pull them.

### Question 8

The manufacturer's name is like the "made by" line on a toy — it tells you which company built the medicine.

### Question 9

"Rx only" is like a "members only" sign — you need a doctor's permission (a prescription) to get this medicine, unlike cough drops you can just buy.

### Question 10

A controlled-substance marker is like a special lock on certain medicines — because they can be misused, the government keeps extra rules about how they are ordered, stored, and counted.

### Question 11

This warning is like a fence around a swimming pool — it reminds adults to keep the medicine where small children cannot reach and accidentally swallow it.

### Question 12

Storage instructions are like the "keep refrigerated" note on a yogurt cup — the medicine only stays good if you keep it at the right temperature.

### Question 13

"Ophthalmic" is the doctor-word for "eye." This label is like a sign that says "eyes only" so nobody uses eye drops in the ear or mouth by mistake.

### Question 14

A liquid concentration is like the label on juice concentrate: it tells you how much "medicine" is packed into each spoonful so you can measure the right amount.

### Question 15

This is like making chocolate milk from powder — you add the amount of water the directions say, shake it, and only then can you pour and measure the drink.

### Question 16

A "shake well" sticker is like the "shake before opening" on orange juice — the good stuff sinks to the bottom, so you stir it up to make every glass the same.

### Question 17

A barcode is like the scanner at the grocery checkout — it reads the exact product so the right medicine ends up with the right person.

### Question 18

This is like a box of crayons that says "24 crayons" — it tells you how many pieces are inside, not how many to use each day.

### Question 19

It's like the safety seal under a jar lid — if the button is already popped or the seal is torn, you know someone opened it, so you don't use it.

### Question 20

OTC medicine is like a grocery item you can buy off the shelf, and its "Drug Facts" label is like the nutrition label that tells you how to use it safely.

### Question 21

A medication order is like a recipe for medicine — it needs the patient, the medicine, how much, how it's given, and how often. The patient's phone number isn't part of that recipe.

### Question 22

PO means "by mouth" and BID means "two times a day." So this recipe says: 500 mg, by mouth, twice a day — like taking two scoops of medicine, morning and night.

### Question 23

QD looks a lot like QID — one little "I" changes "once a day" into "four times a day," like mistaking one cookie for four. That's why we write the word "daily" instead.

### Question 24

The little "q" means "every," so q4h means "every 4 hours" — like setting a timer that goes off every four hours.

### Question 25

PRN is like "take it only when your head hurts" — you don't have to take it on a schedule, but you also can't take it more often than every 6 hours.

### Question 26

"Stat" is the doctor's way of saying "right now!" — like when a coach yells for the ball immediately during a play.

### Question 27

NPO is like "no snacks allowed" — the stomach has to be empty, so nothing goes in the mouth, not even a sip of water.

### Question 28

SL means the medicine goes under the tongue and melts there, like a breath mint that dissolves instead of being swallowed.

### Question 29

IM means the medicine goes into a muscle, like a shot in the arm — "intra" means inside and "muscular" means muscle.

### Question 30

Topical means "on the outside" — like rubbing lotion on your skin, not putting it in your mouth.

### Question 31

Medicine that's a liquid with tiny solid bits settles like mud in a jar — you shake it so every spoonful has the same amount of medicine.

### Question 32

Using two identifiers is like a two-key lock — you need both the name and the birth date to be sure the medicine is for the right person.

### Question 33

Checking an order against the MAR is like checking a grocery list against your cart — every item has to match before you're done.

### Question 34

A medication order needs the doctor's signature like a check needs your parent's signature — it proves the person in charge really approved it.

### Question 35

The DEA number is like a special license plate that shows a doctor is allowed to order the extra-regulated medicines.

### Question 36

Refills are like "refill coupons" on a coffee card — when they run out, the patient needs the doctor to write a new one.

### Question 37

"Take as directed" is like a teacher saying "do the homework" without telling you which page — you don't actually know what to do.

### Question 38

"ac" means "before chow" — before eating. "pc" means after eating. Easy to remember if you think of ac first in the alphabet coming before pc.

### Question 39

The dose is the "how much" — 10 mg — just like a recipe telling you how many cups of flour to add.

### Question 40

IV tells you the medicine goes straight into a vein — the "road" the medicine travels, not the amount.

### Question 41

BID is the "how often" — twice a day, like brushing your teeth morning and night.

### Question 42

E-prescribing is like typing a text instead of writing in messy cursive — the message is clear, and the computer can double-check for mistakes.

### Question 43

Two tablets a day for ten days is like two cookies a day for ten days — that's twenty cookies in total.

### Question 44

An MDI is like a spray bottle that squirts a measured puff of medicine you breathe into your lungs.

### Question 45

Route is like the difference between sunscreen and juice — sunscreen goes on your skin, never in your mouth.

### Question 46

mg and mcg are like dollars and pennies — one dollar is 1,000 pennies. Writing the wrong one is like charging 1,000 dollars instead of one dollar.

### Question 47

mL is like counting how many cups of water, while mg is like counting how much sugar is dissolved in the water — different things.

### Question 48

Once you mix the powder with water, the medicine is like fresh juice — it only stays good for a certain number of days, then you throw it out.

### Question 49

Some pills are like a timed-release capsule — if you crush it, all the medicine rushes out at once instead of slowly, which can be dangerous.

### Question 50

An extended-release pill is like a slow-drip water bottle that releases a little medicine all day instead of all at once.

### Question 51

A blank dose is like a recipe that forgot the amount of flour — you can't bake the cake until someone tells you how much to add.

### Question 52

Without the route, you don't know the "road" the medicine takes — by mouth, into a vein, into a muscle — so you have to ask.

### Question 53

If the order doesn't say how often, it's like a workout plan that forgot how many times a week to exercise — you have to ask before you start.

### Question 54

If you can't read a note, you ask the person who wrote it — you never guess what a messy word says, especially when it's medicine.

### Question 55

A lowercase "u" looks a lot like a zero, so "10U" could be read as "100." Writing "units" out avoids that mix-up.

### Question 56

Writing 1.0 is like putting an extra zero on a price tag — if the decimal dot gets lost, $1.0 looks like $10. Leave the trailing zero off.

### Question 57

Always put a zero in front of the decimal — 0.5 — like putting a "0" before the dot so nobody misses the dot and thinks it's 5.

### Question 58

Hydralazine and hydroxyzine sound like twins with very similar names but do totally different jobs — like confusing a baker and a banker because the words look alike.

### Question 59

If a letter is in the wrong mailbox, you don't deliver it to whoever is nearby — you find the right mailbox first.

### Question 60

Expired medicine is like spoiled food — even if it looks fine, you don't serve it; you follow the rules for throwing it away.

### Question 61

If a recipe called for ten cups of salt, you'd double-check with the cook before pouring — an assistant double-checks a surprising dose with the prescriber.

### Question 62

One tiny letter changes "once a day" into "four times a day" — you never flip a coin on that; you ask the person who wrote it.

### Question 63

Only the person in charge of the recipe can fix it — you ask the doctor or nurse, not a neighbor.

### Question 64

A verbal order is like a phone message — you repeat it back to be sure you heard every number and word correctly.

### Question 65

Documenting a change is like writing a corrected note on the recipe card so the next person uses the right amounts too.

### Question 66

"Continue home medications" is like a note that says "keep doing what you were doing" without saying what that was.

### Question 67

An order with no name is like a birthday card with no name on it — you can't deliver it until you know who it's for.

### Question 68

An order without a signature is like a check without a signature — the bank won't cash it, and the office shouldn't use it.

### Question 69

If the recipe's ingredient amounts don't add up, you ask the chef — you don't quietly change the numbers yourself.

### Question 70

If a price tag might say $1.5 or $15, you ask before paying — with medicine, the wrong guess could be ten times too much.

### Question 71

SC, SQ, and SL look a lot alike when written fast, so writing the word out keeps everyone on the same page.

### Question 72

Two words that look alike can mean very different things — you ask which one was meant instead of guessing.

### Question 73

Mixing medicine is like following a recipe's water line exactly — you check the label or ask the expert, you don't eyeball it.

### Question 74

If you can't read whether the carton says 250 or 500, you check the fine print or ask — you don't guess, because one is double the other.

### Question 75

Similar boxes are like identical-looking twins — you check their full names, not their matching outfits.

### Question 76

An extended-release pill is like a timed-release capsule — cutting it is like smashing the timer so all the medicine dumps out at once.

### Question 77

The assistant is like a referee who spots a problem and blows the whistle — the referee doesn't play the game or decide the score.

### Question 78

The "rights" are like a pre-flight checklist — the pilot checks every item every time, not just the fuel.

### Question 79

The five rights are like five locks on a treasure chest — every one has to be checked before you open it.

### Question 80

If the name on the medicine doesn't match the person, you stop — like a letter carrier who won't deliver a package to the wrong house.

### Question 81

For medicine questions, you ask the medicine expert — the pharmacist — just like you'd ask a mechanic about your car.

### Question 82

A "daily" policy is like a school rule to write your name clearly — it exists so nobody misreads what you meant.

### Question 83

81 mg and 325 mg are like a small and a large battery — you match the size the order calls for, not whatever is closest.

### Question 84

When the coffee card's free refills run out, you can't just keep getting free coffee — the manager (the doctor) has to approve more.

### Question 85

If the fire alarm goes off but you can't reach the chief, you tell the next person in charge right away — you don't wait or guess.
